title: Accessibility & reading tools
summary: Adjust text, colors, spacing and motion; open reading view, listen with a device voice and find access help. Our approach to useful, respectful access information.

Find “Accessibility & reading” just below the navigation, or “Reading tools” in the footer. The tools are optional, and you can reset your choices any time. Make the page work for you Open reading tools The optional controls need JavaScript. Your browser’s zoom, reader mode and device access settings remain available. Text & colorsEnlarge text up to 200%, choose a plain typeface, add space between letters, words and lines, or underline links. Choose light or dark high contrast, warm paper, or the original colors. Photographs and communication pictures keep their colors. Movement & touchReduce animation and pause autoplay media. Your device’s reduced-motion setting is also respected. Make controls larger, or use a reading line that follows your pointer or a tap beside text. A keyboard slider adjusts its position too. A quieter reading viewOpen a simpler view of the page’s text, links and image descriptions. Copy or print the reading text. Forms, planners and other interactive tools remain on the original page; return there to use them or open collapsed sections. Listen at your paceIn reading view, expand “Listen, copy or print.” Choose a device voice and speed, then select “Read aloud.” You can pause, continue or stop; continuing restarts the current passage. Closing reading view stops speech.This feature is available only when your browser provides a voice identified as local to your device. If no voice is available, use your device’s spoken-content tools. Keyboard & finding your placeUse Tab and Shift + Tab to move between controls, Enter or Space to activate buttons, and arrow keys for native choices. Escape closes the tools and returns you to the opening button. Use “Skip to main content” or choose a heading under “Jump to a section.” Your choices, your deviceSettings start off unsaved. “Remember my choices on this device” keeps them in this browser for other pages and visits. Uncheck it or choose “Reset all choices” to remove the saved settings. Leave it off on a shared device.Reading tools & privacy Use the access tools you already know Browser zoom, pinch-to-zoom, screen readers, keyboard navigation, voice control, switch access and your device’s display settings can be used alongside these choices. If this browser cannot open the panel, use browser zoom or reader mode and your device’s accessibility settings. Optional controls are one part of making this site usable. Some pages, embedded media and interactive tools may still have barriers. We have not completed an independent accessibility audit. If something gets in your way, email us about access. The page link and a brief description help; sharing your device, browser or assistive technology is optional. You do not need to share a diagnosis or private care information. The details that make an outing possible “Accessible” can mean almost nothing until somebody tells you about the hill, the gravel, the elevator, the lighting, the quiet corner, the restroom and the walk from the car. This is the standard we use when researching calendar events, Favorite Places and practical guides. We look for current official information first, then use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when they add useful lived detail. We label uncertainty instead of turning it into a promise. What we checkEight questions before “accessible.”Not every venue publishes every answer. An honest “not confirmed” is more useful than a confident guess. Wheelchair + adaptive strollerStep-free entrances, ramps, elevators, doorway routes, seating, transfer points, wheelchair or mobility-device rentals and whether the route actually works beyond the lobby. Terrain + distancePavement, packed gravel, loose gravel, grass, roots, slopes, long walks, mud, snow and places where a wheeled mobility device may need more help than a general accessibility label suggests. Sensory + communicationNoise, lighting, crowd density, smells, startling effects, quiet spaces, sensory kits, visual supports, AAC-friendly participation, flexible movement, re-entry and whether “sensory-friendly” changes the environment or only the schedule. Blind + low-vision accessBraille, large print, tactile or verbal description, audio description, contrast, wayfinding and lighting changes. We avoid assuming that a wheelchair-accessible route is also an accessible visual experience. Deaf + hard-of-hearing accessCaptions, ASL interpretation, assistive-listening systems, visual announcements, hearing loops/headsets and how far in advance an accommodation must be requested. Restrooms + practical careAccessible and family restrooms, changing tables, and an adult-size or height-adjustable changing table only when a venue specifically publishes that information. We never imply that a particular family uses a facility simply because we report that it exists. Parking + arrivalAccessible spaces, drop-off, distance to the entrance, the best door to use, city parking realities, whether a shuttle runs and what happens after dark. Weather + escape planOutdoor exposure, snow, ice, rain, heat, muddy paths, low light, indoor backup options, break spaces and how easy it is to shorten the visit or leave. Evidence labels How strong is the information? Organizer-confirmedA current event page, ticket page, venue policy or direct accessibility statement. This is our starting point. Venue access guideA current accessibility, visitor, trail, seating or building guide that adds detail beyond the event listing. Public visitor reportA review or public Q&A can reveal practical realities—steepness, crowd bottlenecks, muddy ground, stroller frustration—but it is anecdotal and dated. We label it as such and do not let it override newer official information. Not confirmedWe looked and did not find a reliable current answer. That is a prompt to contact the venue, not permission to guess. See the method in useThe calendar now carries the field notes.Each dated listing can include mobility, terrain, sensory conditions, vision/hearing supports, restrooms, changing-equipment status, parking, weather, a map and a five-step visual visit card.Open the accessible New England calendar ↗ Editorial rules What we will not do. We do not convert “ADA accessible” into a blanket promise about the whole experience. We do not assume a venue has an adult-size changing table, sensory room, ASL interpreter, elevator or smooth terrain unless we can confirm it. We do not present a visitor review as a verified current venue policy. We date access research because buildings, programs, construction, staffing and weather conditions change. We do not diagnose what a person “should” need. The information is there so each reader can decide what matters for their own visit. The website itself Access should apply here, too. We aim for readable type, strong contrast, keyboard-accessible navigation, useful headings, meaningful link text, alt text for informative images, layouts that work on smaller screens, and controls that do not rely on color alone. Visual planners are editable because one person’s helpful wording or picture can be another person’s clutter. Our tools use visible words alongside icons, large controls, familiar examples, keyboard access and clear optional sections. Preselected settings make it possible to finish without adjusting every detail. Color choices always have written names; color alone does not carry an instruction. Our creative standardBeautiful, useful, respectful.Our default look is preppy New England: Nantucket light, Vermont warmth, recognizable objects and natural materials. Communication pictures keep a clear subject and a familiar word. Decoration belongs around the task, where it can add pleasure without obscuring meaning.We create and publish lawful, family-friendly content. Sexual content, graphic violence, hate imagery, exploitation, harassment and deceptive images of real people have no place here. We respect privacy, consent, intellectual property and the dignity of the people we portray. AI-created illustrations are identified as such and are never presented as family photographs or evidence about a real venue.The picture-card studio currently offers a reviewed starter collection and private, in-tab photo selection. It has no public upload gallery and does not generate new images live. Personal photos are not sent to us or automatically inspected. Use only appropriate pictures you are permitted to use. Any future live image-generation service must include input and output moderation before it is made available. If a page is difficult to use—or a field note is wrong, stale or missing—please contact us with the page and the detail that needs attention.

title: Accessible Ice Cream: New England, at our family’s pace.

title: A scoop, a phone, and a choice.
summary: An ordinary ice cream outing at Rancatore’s in Lexington, a real flavor-case photo and a family-made choice board. Practical ideas for families and independent scoop shops.

The choice belongs to the customerA case full of ice cream offers plenty to choose from. The question we brought to Ranc’s was how to put those choices in a form James could consider.We were heading to Rancatore’s in downtown Lexington—Ranc’s, as we call it—and I had my phone with me. James, my 14-year-old son, is autistic and non-speaking. He communicates in ways that include pointing and using his iPad, so clear pictures are part of our everyday life.We had already made a little visual board to choose where to go. Ranc’s, Cookie Monstah, and Wilson Farm each had their own picture. Once we reached the ice cream shop, there was another decision waiting for us: the flavors.Rather than try to recite the entire case out loud, I photographed the actual displays and shared them with AI. The idea was simple: bring the choices off the labels and onto a screen we could look at together.Our finished page was not a perfect menu or a finished communication system. It was a first attempt that needed checking. The photographs below show the source and the original result, including the parts we would simplify another time.We ended up with a photo just outside, an ice cream cone in hand. That ordinary afternoon—not the technology—is the point of the story.From the family notebookThe simple idea.A phone photograph can be a starting point. AI was one tool we tried for arranging the options; it is not a requirement.01Photograph the real, current options.02Show pictures the person recognizes.03Check, simplify, then leave room to choose—or decline.The support is new. James’s own communication methods are not.The practical version for another outing → A small experiment, right at the counterFrom the flavor case to the flavor board.These are the real photographs and the original combined choice board we made during our outing.01 / The source photographRealWe started with what was physically in the shop, not a generic ice cream menu.02 / The visual choice boardAIThe complete combined cone-and-flavor choice board from our outing, in its original arrangement. The AI-illustrated flavors still need checking against the actual case.The photographs document what we saw. The AI illustrations are an attempted translation, not independent confirmation of the labels, ingredients or choices available. Do not use this example as a current menu. A cup or a cone. Before the ice cream counterFirst we chose where to go.We started with a visual destination board: Cookie Monstah in Burlington, Ranc’s in Lexington and Wilson Farm in Lexington. Each place had a familiar storefront picture rather than a generic picture of a cookie or an ice cream.Then, at Ranc’s, we made the combined cone-and-flavor board shown above. Its original layout keeps three cone choices at the top and the labeled flavors below. Another version could show these separately rather than presenting everything at once.The technology wasn’t making the choice for James. It was helping us show him the choices.Our original three-place destination storyboard, without redesigning it. A few things I learnedFast doesn’t mean finished.The AI was quick, but it wasn't automatically right. It can invent a flavor, misread a handwritten label, or make a beautifully crowded page. Our large flavor board was a first pass; a shorter display of the choices James wanted to consider might be easier to navigate.The real photos gave us something concrete to check. The board was never meant to replace James’s established augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) supports, or his ability to say no, ask for something different, or take a break.Sometimes the best visual is simply the photograph you already took. A picture cannot establish ingredients or allergen safety: ask staff about ingredients and cross-contact rather than inferring either from a label or illustration.An optional tool, not the whole methodA prompt to try.“Use these photos to make a draft picture choice board. Copy only labels you can read clearly, and flag anything uncertain instead of guessing. Do not add flavors, cone types or ingredient claims. Use clear labels and leave space to separate the flavor choice from the container choice.”A careful prompt is not a guarantee. Check every option against the current display and staff guidance before using the result. Remove unavailable items and change pictures or labels that do not suit the person.No AI needed: use a checked photo of a few actual options, or arrange your own photographs. Avoid capturing other customers or uploading private information. For your next scoopBring the choices closer. Keep the outing ordinary.This is what we would take from our Ranc’s experiment into another visit. Adapt the idea to the person—not the person to the board.Start with today’s options.Ask what is available, then use clear photographs or familiar pictures. Our old flavor board is a record of an experiment, not a shopping list for your visit. Check ingredients separately with staff.Make one question manageable.Try flavor and cup-or-cone as separate choices. Start with a manageable display while keeping a way to ask for other options. A shorter board should not silently remove the person’s right to choose something else.Leave time—and room for “no.”Keep the person’s usual communication available. Accept pointing, a device, speech or another familiar response without turning ordering into a test. Changing a choice, taking a break and declining are choices, too.Let a scoop be enough.Decide where eating will work and how to finish the visit. You do not need a second activity or a perfect photograph to make an ice cream stop worthwhile.Start with the free editable picture cards ↓These are family planning ideas, not an individualized communication assessment. It is whether a customer can find out what is available, take the time they need and communicate a choice in their own way.Keep choices current.A simple, current picture menu or clear photo of available flavors can be worth trying. Use readable labels, mark sold-out items and check information with staff. Pictures should not substitute for ingredient and allergy information.Welcome the customer’s tools.Address the customer, not only the person accompanying them. Make room for a phone, communication device or picture board, and ask what assistance would be useful rather than assuming.Offer another way to look.When feasible, let someone consider the choices away from the immediate ordering position without losing their opportunity to order. Do not assume that a customer who needs more time needs fewer choices.Describe what you actually offer.Share concrete details about ordering, seating, entrances and any verified quiet-hour arrangements. title: A little Easter color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.
search: The journalBerlin, MassachusettsAn Easter field note The bunny had a few photo ideas of its own. A spring visit to Berlin FarmsA little Easter color.An egg hunt, a bunny with a few good poses, and a family photograph worth keeping.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier Easter visitPastel eggs across the lawn. White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. The family storyMap & visit detailsAccess & sensory notesMore photographs Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good part is right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door.
